questions.stem: Section 9(1) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) sets out the purposes for which a sentence may be imposed. Which of these is one of them?
options: To make it clear that the community denounces the offender's conduct
To compensate the victim fully for every financial loss the offence caused
To raise revenue for the state to fund police and the courts
To give the victim the power to decide the offender's punishment
questions.explanation: Section 9(1) lists punishment that is just in all the circumstances, rehabilitation, deterrence, recognising the harm done to a victim, denunciation and community protection, or a combination of them. Compensation orders exist, but full compensation is not a purpose of sentencing, and victims do not decide sentences.

questions.stem: Retribution, as a theory of punishment, holds that:
options: an offender should meet the victim and agree on how to repair the harm
an offender should receive punishment proportionate to the wrong they have done
an offender should be treated so they no longer want to commit further offences
an offender should be removed from society so they cannot reoffend
questions.explanation: Retribution is 'just deserts': punishment matching the seriousness of the crime, reflected in s 9(1)(a) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld). Treatment describes rehabilitation, removal describes prevention or incapacitation, and meeting the victim describes restorative justice.

questions.stem: A judge sentencing a man for repeated drink driving says the sentence must show other drivers that they too will be punished severely. The judge is emphasising:
options: general deterrence
specific deterrence
rehabilitation
retribution
questions.explanation: General deterrence aims to discourage other people in the community from committing similar offences. Specific deterrence targets the offender in front of the court, so that they do not reoffend.

questions.stem: Sentencing a man with many convictions for violent offences, a judge imposes a long prison term and says the community must be kept safe from him. Which purpose is the judge emphasising?
options: Restorative justice
Recognition of the victim
Protection of the community
Rehabilitation of the offender
questions.explanation: Protecting the Queensland community from the offender is a purpose in s 9(1)(e) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld). Imprisonment achieves this by incapacitation (prevention) while the offender is in custody. Rehabilitation aims to change the offender's behaviour.

questions.stem: One purpose of sentencing in section 9(1) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) is to recognise the harm done by the offender to a victim of the offence. Which statement best describes its effect?
options: Victims now decide the length of the sentence in all serious cases
Courts must now order compensation in every case in which a victim was harmed
Victims may now appeal against a sentence directly to the Court of Appeal
Courts may impose a sentence partly to acknowledge the harm the victim suffered
questions.explanation: Paragraph (ca) lets a court impose a sentence to recognise the harm done to a victim, alongside punishment, rehabilitation, deterrence, denunciation and protection. Victims inform the court about harm, often through the prosecutor or a victim impact statement, but they do not set the sentence or bring sentence appeals.

questions.stem: Recidivism refers to:
options: an offender committing further offences after being dealt with for an earlier offence
a sentence that is served at the same time as another sentence for a different offence
a sentence that is suspended so the offender does not go to prison immediately
a process in which the offender and victim meet to repair the harm caused
questions.explanation: Recidivism, or reoffending, is a key measure of whether sentences achieve rehabilitation and specific deterrence. Sentences served at the same time are concurrent, and meetings between offender and victim are restorative justice processes.

questions.stem: Restorative justice is best described as an approach that:
options: keeps the offender in prison until they have been fully restored to good mental health
requires the offender to pay back the state for the cost of investigating the offence
restores the offender's right to vote and work once they have served their sentence
brings the offender, victim and community together to repair the harm caused
questions.explanation: Restorative justice focuses on accountability and repairing harm, often through a facilitated conference where the offender hears the effect of the offence and agrees to make amends. In Queensland, restorative justice processes are used particularly for young offenders under the Youth Justice Act 1992 (Qld).

questions.stem: In a Court of Appeal sentencing judgment, the ratio decidendi is:
options: the summary of facts agreed between the prosecution and defence
the legal reasoning essential to the decision, which binds lower courts
remarks made in passing that are persuasive but never binding on courts
the sentence imposed on the offender, stated at the end of the judgment
questions.explanation: The ratio decidendi is the reason for the decision and binds lower courts in the same hierarchy under the doctrine of precedent. Obiter dicta are remarks 'by the way' that may persuade later courts but do not bind them.

questions.stem: In a sentence appeal about a stealing offence, a Court of Appeal judge comments on how she would approach sentencing for a fraud offence, which was not before the court. This comment is:
options: a victim impact statement, which must be considered when sentencing fraud
obiter dicta, which may be persuasive in later cases but is not binding
ratio decidendi, which binds every court in Queensland on fraud sentences
a guideline judgment, which every court must follow for fraud offences
questions.explanation: A comment on a matter not necessary to decide the case is obiter dicta. It may influence later courts, but it is not binding. A guideline judgment is a formal judgment given by the Court of Appeal under Part 2A of the Act.

questions.stem: Section 9(2)(a) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) requires a court to have regard to the principles that:
options: imprisonment is a last resort, and a sentence letting the offender stay in the community is preferable
imprisonment is the starting point for every indictable offence unless the offender has pleaded guilty
every offender must receive the maximum penalty if they have any previous convictions
a fine is the only appropriate sentence for an offender with no previous convictions
questions.explanation: These two principles reflect the cost and harm of imprisonment and the value of rehabilitation in the community. They do not mean prison is never used; they are weighed with all the other matters in s 9(2), and they do not apply to some offences, such as those involving violence.

questions.stem: Jack is sentenced for an assault that caused physical harm to a stranger. How does section 9 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) change the court's approach?
options: The court must impose imprisonment, because all offences involving violence carry a mandatory prison term
The court must apply the last resort principle more strictly, because the victim was a stranger
The court must ignore Jack's personal circumstances, because only the victim's views are relevant
The last resort principle does not apply, and the court must focus primarily on community safety
questions.explanation: Under s 9(2A) and (3), the last resort principles do not apply to offences involving violence or resulting in physical harm. The court must have regard primarily to matters such as the risk of harm to the community, the victim's circumstances and the violence used, but it still considers the offender's antecedents, age and remorse. Prison is not mandatory.

questions.stem: Under section 9(10) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), an offender's previous convictions:
options: must be treated as aggravating if reasonable, given their nature, relevance and age
must be ignored, because the offender has already been punished for those earlier offences
must be treated as mitigating, because they show the offender needs rehabilitation
may be considered only if the offender pleads not guilty to the current offence
questions.explanation: Section 9(10) requires each previous conviction to be treated as an aggravating factor if it can reasonably be, having regard to its nature, its relevance to the current offence and the time since it was recorded. Old or unrelated convictions may carry little weight.

questions.stem: Bella committed an assault while heavily drunk and argues this should reduce her sentence. Under the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), the court will:
options: reduce the sentence only if she has no previous convictions at all
not treat her voluntary intoxication as a mitigating factor
reduce the sentence, because intoxication lessens her responsibility
treat her intoxication as a complete defence and dismiss the charge
questions.explanation: Section 9(9A) provides that voluntary intoxication by alcohol or drugs is not a mitigating factor in sentencing. Intoxication can sometimes be relevant at trial to whether a specific intent existed, but that is a different question from sentence.

questions.stem: An offender is sentenced for an assault on his partner. Under the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), the fact that the offence is a domestic violence offence:
options: must be treated as aggravating, unless exceptional circumstances make that unreasonable
must be treated as mitigating, because the offence occurred inside a private family home
is irrelevant to sentence, because it is not an element of the offence of assault itself
means the court must transfer the case to the Murri Court for sentencing
questions.explanation: Section 9(10A) requires a court to treat the domestic violence character of an offence as aggravating, unless exceptional circumstances make that unreasonable. Separately, s 9(10B) requires an offender's own experience as a victim of domestic violence to be treated as mitigating in relevant cases.

questions.stem: Which is a mitigating factor that would usually reduce a sentence?
options: The victim was elderly and particularly vulnerable to harm
The offence was planned carefully over several weeks
The offender pleaded guilty early and showed genuine remorse
The offender used a weapon during the commission of the offence
questions.explanation: An early guilty plea and genuine remorse reduce culpability or the need for deterrence and save the cost of a trial. Use of a weapon, a vulnerable victim and planning all increase the seriousness of the offence and are aggravating factors.

questions.stem: Under section 13 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), a court sentencing an offender who pleaded guilty:
options: may not reduce the sentence if the evidence against the offender was strong
must record no conviction, because a guilty plea shows that the offender is remorseful
must consider the plea and may reduce the sentence, having regard to when it was entered
must reduce the sentence by exactly one-third, regardless of when the plea was entered in court
questions.explanation: Section 13 requires the plea to be taken into account and allows a reduction having regard to its timing, so an early plea usually earns a greater reduction. If the court does not reduce the sentence it must say so and give reasons in open court. There is no fixed fraction in the Act.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old university student with no criminal history pleads guilty to a minor stealing offence. Under section 12 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), what must the court consider in deciding whether to record a conviction?
options: The nature of the offence, his character and age, and the impact on his chances of employment
Only whether the victim wants a conviction to be recorded against the offender
Only the maximum penalty for stealing, because recording is automatic for indictable offences
Whether he can afford a fine, because a conviction is recorded only if a fine is unpaid
questions.explanation: Section 12(2) directs the court to all the circumstances, including the nature of the offence, the offender's character and age, and the impact of a conviction on their economic or social wellbeing or chances of finding employment. A conviction not recorded is generally not a conviction for any purpose.

questions.stem: When sentencing an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander offender, section 9(2) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) requires the court to have regard to:
options: a fixed reduction in sentence that applies to every Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander offender
the requirement that the offender be sentenced only in a remote community court
cultural considerations and any submissions from a representative of the community justice group
the views of the offender's family only, instead of the usual sentencing principles
questions.explanation: Section 9(2)(oa) and (p) require regard to cultural considerations, including the effect of systemic disadvantage and intergenerational trauma, and to relevant submissions by a community justice group representative. These are factors weighed with all others, not an automatic discount.

questions.stem: Under section 19 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), a court that considers no punishment or only a nominal punishment is appropriate may release an offender on a recognisance (a good behaviour bond). Which statement is correct?
options: A conviction must be recorded, and the offender must serve a short prison term first
The offender must perform at least 40 hours of unpaid community service work
The offender is supervised by a corrective services officer who visits each week
No conviction is recorded, and the good behaviour period is up to 3 years
questions.explanation: An order under s 19 is made without recording a conviction, and the offender must be of good behaviour and appear if called on during a period of up to three years. If the offender breaches it, the court may forfeit the recognisance and sentence them for the original offence.

questions.stem: In deciding the amount of a fine, section 48 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) requires a court, as far as practicable, to take into account:
options: the amount the victim has asked the court to impose on the offender
the average fine imposed on all offenders in Queensland that year
the offender's financial circumstances and the burden of paying it
the cost to the state of investigating and prosecuting the offence
questions.explanation: Section 48 requires courts to consider the offender's financial circumstances and the burden of paying, so that a fine is a fair penalty for people on different incomes. A fine is paid to the state, not set by the victim.

questions.stem: Which statement about a probation order in Queensland is correct?
options: The offender serves the whole sentence in prison but may leave for work during the day
The offender performs 40 to 240 hours of unpaid work but has no other conditions at all
The offender is released with no supervision and only has to pay a sum of money
The offender is supervised in the community for 6 months to 3 years and must not reoffend
questions.explanation: Under ss 92-93 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), probation is supervision by a corrective services officer for between 6 months and 3 years, with requirements such as not reoffending, reporting and attending programs. Unpaid work with a 40 to 240 hour range is a community service order.

questions.stem: A court is considering a community service order for an offender. Under the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), the order:
options: can be made only if the offender is also sentenced to a term of imprisonment
requires the offender to live in a community residential facility for the whole order
is for 40 to 240 hours of unpaid work, and usually needs the offender's agreement
is for up to 1,000 hours of unpaid work, which must be completed in five years
questions.explanation: Section 103 sets the range at 40 to 240 hours, generally to be performed within one year, and s 106 says the court may make the order only if the offender agrees, apart from orders required by s 108B. The court must also be satisfied the offender is suitable.

questions.stem: A court imposes 10 months' imprisonment but orders that it be served by way of an intensive correction order. Which statement best describes the offender's situation?
options: No conviction is recorded and the offender is released without any supervision or conditions
The offender serves the first half in prison and the remainder in the community on parole
The offender must serve the whole term in prison but may be released early for good behaviour
A conviction is recorded, and the term is served in the community under strict conditions
questions.explanation: An ICO can be made only where imprisonment of 1 year or less is imposed, and only if a conviction is recorded. The offender serves the sentence in the community, reporting at least twice a week and doing up to 12 hours a week of programs and community service (ss 111-114).

questions.stem: Ali receives 18 months' imprisonment, wholly suspended for an operational period of 2 years. Eight months later he commits a new offence punishable by imprisonment. What is the most likely result under the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld)?
options: Nothing, because a suspended sentence can never be activated once it has been imposed
The court must extend the operational period, because activation is never permitted
The court may only fine him, because the original offence has already been punished
The court must order him to serve the whole suspended term, unless it would be unjust
questions.explanation: A suspended sentence (available for imprisonment of 5 years or less) is served only if the offender commits an offence punishable by imprisonment during the operational period. Section 147(2) then requires the court to order the whole term to be served unless it considers that unjust, for example because the new offence is trivial.

questions.stem: Kim pleads guilty in a Magistrates Court to stealing offences driven by a severe methamphetamine addiction. Which Queensland order is designed for offenders like Kim?
options: A good behaviour bond without conviction, which cannot include any treatment conditions
An intensive correction order, which requires the offender to live in a drug rehabilitation centre
A serious violent offence declaration, which delays parole until most of the term is served
A drug and alcohol treatment order, combining a suspended prison term with intensive treatment
questions.explanation: A drug and alcohol treatment order under Part 8A suits offenders with a severe substance use disorder that contributed to the offence. It has a custodial part (imprisonment of 4 years or less, suspended) and a rehabilitation part with treatment, testing and court supervision, and the offender must agree to it.

questions.stem: An offender is sentenced to 2 years for burglary and 1 year for stealing, and the court orders the terms to be served concurrently. How long is the total period of imprisonment?
options: 2 years
3 years
1 year
18 months
questions.explanation: Concurrent sentences are served at the same time, so the total is the longest term, 2 years. Under s 155 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) sentences are concurrent unless the court orders otherwise; cumulative sentences (s 156) would total 3 years.

questions.stem: When a court orders sentences to be served cumulatively, it must still consider whether the total sentence is just and appropriate for the offending as a whole. This is called the:
options: last resort principle
proportionality of parole
totality principle
parity principle
questions.explanation: The totality principle guards against a crushing overall sentence when several terms are added together. The parity principle concerns similar sentences for co-offenders with similar culpability, and the last resort principle relates to choosing imprisonment at all.

questions.stem: A Queensland court sentences an offender to 2 years' imprisonment for a property offence. Which statement about parole is correct?
options: The court must fix a parole eligibility date at 80% of the term, because the offender was imprisoned
The Parole Board decides the release date, because courts cannot make any order about parole
The court must fix a parole release date, as the term is 3 years or less and not violent or sexual
The offender must serve the full 2 years, because parole is not available for property offences
questions.explanation: Under s 160B of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), for a sentence of 3 years or less that is not for a serious violent or sexual offence, the court generally fixes a parole release date. For longer sentences the court fixes a parole eligibility date, and the 80% rule applies only to serious violent offences.

questions.stem: An offender is sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment for a serious assault listed in Schedule 1 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld). What follows?
options: The court must make a serious violent offence declaration, so parole comes only after 80%
The court may choose whether to make a declaration, and he becomes eligible for parole halfway
He is eligible for parole immediately, because a long sentence shows rehabilitation is needed
He must serve the whole term, because offenders convicted of violent offences are never paroled
questions.explanation: If an offender is sentenced to 10 years or more for a Schedule 1 offence, the court must make a serious violent offence declaration (s 161B(1)). Under s 182 of the Corrective Services Act 2006 (Qld), parole eligibility then comes after 80% of the term or 15 years, whichever is less. For terms of 5 to under 10 years a declaration is discretionary.

questions.stem: What is the penalty for murder in Queensland under section 305 of the Criminal Code?
options: A fixed term of 30 years' imprisonment, with no possibility of parole
Mandatory life imprisonment, with parole eligibility after at least 20 years
Up to 25 years' imprisonment, with parole eligibility at the halfway point
Life imprisonment or a suspended sentence, at the discretion of the judge
questions.explanation: Section 305 makes life imprisonment mandatory for murder (or an indefinite sentence), and under the Corrective Services Act 2006 (Qld) the usual parole eligibility is after 20 years. Longer minimums apply in some cases, such as multiple murders (30 years) or killing a police officer (25 years).

questions.stem: Which is a function of the Queensland Sentencing Advisory Council?
options: Researching sentencing and informing the community about sentencing matters
Deciding the sentences imposed in serious cases in the District Court
Hearing appeals against sentences imposed by magistrates and judges
Deciding when prisoners are released on parole after their eligibility date
questions.explanation: Under Part 12 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld), the council advises the Attorney-General when asked, gives views to the Court of Appeal on guideline judgments, researches and publishes information on sentencing and seeks community views. It does not sentence offenders or decide parole.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Murri Court in Queensland is correct?
options: It is a sentencing court in which Elders or Respected Persons give the magistrate cultural advice
It is a trial court in which a jury of Elders decides whether the defendant is guilty
It is a separate court that hears all offences, including murder, committed by Aboriginal people
It is a tribunal that replaces criminal sentences with traditional punishment ordered by Elders
questions.explanation: The Murri Court operates within Magistrates and Childrens Courts as a culturally appropriate sentencing court for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander defendants who plead guilty. Elders or Respected Persons help the magistrate understand the defendant's circumstances, but the magistrate imposes the sentence under ordinary sentencing law.

questions.stem: A defendant tells his lawyer he is not guilty of the charge but would like his case heard in the Murri Court. Which response is most accurate?
options: The Murri Court is for defendants who plead or intend to plead guilty, so his trial would be in the ordinary court
He can have his trial in the Murri Court, because it hears all charges against Aboriginal defendants
He must plead guilty, because Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander defendants cannot have a trial
His case will go to the Murri Court only if the victim also identifies as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander
questions.explanation: Referral to the Murri Court requires a guilty plea, or an intention to plead guilty, and the defendant's consent to take part. A defendant who maintains innocence has the right to a trial in the ordinary court, and nobody is required to plead guilty.

questions.stem: A report shows that many people released from short prison sentences in Queensland return to prison within two years. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Short prison terms may achieve little rehabilitation or specific deterrence for these offenders
Short prison terms are fully effective because the offenders were punished for their crimes
Courts should stop considering rehabilitation because it never reduces reoffending
The return to prison proves that community based orders are always less effective
questions.explanation: High return rates suggest short sentences may not address the causes of offending, such as addiction, unemployment, unstable housing or mental illness. This is one argument for programs and community based orders that target those causes; the data alone cannot prove those alternatives are always better.

questions.stem: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are significantly over-represented in Queensland prisons. Which response is most likely to address the underlying causes rather than just the symptoms?
options: Culturally appropriate programs and courts that address disadvantage and reoffending
Longer mandatory prison sentences for all offenders who live in remote communities
Removing cultural considerations from sentencing so every offender is treated identically
Building more prisons in regional areas so that offenders are held closer to home
questions.explanation: Over-representation is linked to systemic disadvantage and intergenerational trauma, which s 9(2)(oa) of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) now requires courts to consider. Culturally appropriate responses such as the Murri Court and community justice groups aim to reduce reoffending; longer sentences and more prisons treat the symptoms.

questions.stem: A critic argues that a sentencing system is effective only if it reduces crime. A supporter of restorative justice would most likely reply that effectiveness should also be judged by:
options: whether the offender is kept away from the community for the whole sentence
whether victims feel heard and offenders take responsibility and repair harm
whether the offender receives the longest sentence available for the offence
whether the sentence is decided quickly without hearing from the victim at all
questions.explanation: Legal criteria for evaluating sentencing include protecting the community, reducing recidivism, meeting the needs of victims, rehabilitating offenders and community confidence. Restorative justice measures success partly by victim satisfaction and the offender's acceptance of responsibility, not only by crime rates.

questions.stem: A government proposes mandatory minimum prison sentences for a common property offence. Which argument against the proposal relies most directly on the principles in section 9 of the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld)?
options: It would increase general deterrence, because offenders would know the minimum penalty in advance
It would reduce the workload of courts, because fewer offenders would contest their charges
It would stop courts tailoring sentences to each offender, against the last resort principle
It would make sentences more consistent, which would increase public confidence in the courts
questions.explanation: Section 9 requires courts to weigh many individual factors and to treat imprisonment as a last resort for non-violent offences. Mandatory minimums remove that discretion and can produce unjust results for less culpable offenders. Consistency and deterrence are arguments for the proposal, not against it.
